accuracy.evidence: Definitions follow AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 and standard texts: skew named by the tail (positive = long right tail), symmetric with matching halves, bimodal with two peaks. Every chart's mean, median and moment skewness were computed in Node before use: naming charts have g1 of +1.04, 0, -1.04, 0 (bimodal), +1.40 and -0.96; build presets +0.77, -0.77 and 0; spot-the-mean charts have mean 3.57 vs median 2, 6.43 vs 8, 3.47 vs 2.5 and 6.53 vs 7.5. The lab's build check needs both the skewness sign and the mean-median order. The adult text states that 'mean on the tail side' is a rule of thumb that can fail for discrete or bimodal data (von Hippel 2005). Numeric items were checked at every corner: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5a-12 has mean a and median 3; 18..26 and 7a-131 has mean a and median 22.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: naming skew after the peak (prediction 1, p3, m7, challenge 'peakside', and a naming-scene message when positive and negative are swapped), assuming mean and median always match (prediction 2, m4, challenge 'alwayssame'), getting the mean's side the wrong way round (spot-the-mean messages, m5, challenge 'wayround'), reading two peaks as an error or one wide group (prediction 3, p4, m6, challenge 'mistake' and 'onegroup') and quoting the mean for skewed pay or prices (p5, challenge 'pulled').

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab works on shape itself: a 9-bar histogram whose bars the learner drags while a live mean line and median line move and a shape check uses moment skewness; a two-group mixture of parkrun times where sliding one group's centre splits one hump into two peaks under a dip test; context cards matched to shapes; and unlabelled mean/median lines on skewed charts. flagbshape (lesson 419) sets a binomial shape from n and p; flagoutlr (781) moves one outlier to choose an average. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_skew.js under 30% similar to every other flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Building the shapes makes the learner see the rule: stretching bars out to the right moves the red mean line past the green median line, and the round only completes when the tail and the order agree; making it symmetric brings them together at 5. In the parkrun scene, walkers 3 minutes slower each step turn one hump (gap 2) into a flat top (gap 3) and then two clear peaks (gap 4+), and sliding back merges them. The text then names what they built.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Peak on the left, tail on the right: what is it called?' (tempting: negative skew, named after the peak; the naming feedback corrects it), 'You stretch a tail to the right: where does the mean go?' (tempting: exactly on the median; the live lines separate) and 'Walkers much slower than runners: what shape?' (tempting: one tall peak; the chart splits into two). Each completion message reveals the learner's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions, each with two tagged wrong answers, and eight distinct messages in SKW.SLIP: peakside (named after the tail, not the peak), tailblind (one side trails off, so not symmetric), wayround (mean pulled towards the tail), alwayssame (they only match when symmetric), mistake (two peaks are two groups, not an error), onegroup (one group gives one wide hump), pulled (high prices drag the mean) and other (the maximum is not typical). The naming and spot scenes add four more reasoned messages.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and define each word as it appears (tail, skewed, bimodal) and pass the learner readability limit; adult paragraphs name the CCSS and AQA statements and key words and pass the adult limit. Canvas labels are dark text on white chips over a pale background and shrink to fit at 390 px; the parkrun minutes labels stay readable on iPhone 13.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs teach one idea each: what shape means and symmetry, skew named by the tail, the mean pulled by the tail with the median as a fair typical value, and bimodal as two groups. Adult paragraphs give the standards, real examples with the rule-of-thumb caveat, four named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate flagged one filler word ('journey'), which was replaced; it found under 12% overlap with every lesson, including 419 and 781.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 (dark) and desktop (light) screenshots of every step at rest, during Show me and finished, plus a wrong challenge answer: the 9 bars fill the canvas width with value labels under them, the mean and median chips sit on separate rows under the axis so they never overlap, the 12 parkrun bars and the runners/minutes/walkers legend fit at 390 px, the four context tiles sit in a 2 by 2 grid with readable text, and the buttons below wrap as 44 px targets.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: four shape buttons for naming and for real data; Bar left and right to pick a bar plus Shorter and Taller (every shape reachable bar by bar); Walkers faster and slower in 3-minute steps; Line A and Line B. Runners and walkers are named in a legend as well as coloured, and the mean and median lines are labelled in text. Every change updates the canvas aria-label (bar height, mean, median, peaks), results go through c.say, and challenge feedback is a polite live region. The walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
